_meta.comment: Hand-authored tips that override the converter's auto-generated tips. Keyed by question id (d1_001, d1_002, ...). Each value is an array of 2-4 short tips. Re-running scripts/convert_test_bank.py merges these into data/domain1.json.

d1_001: Two-sided trap: A says 'IT will pre-audit' — but IT's continuous monitoring is a control activity, not auditing. D says 'auditor can never audit those systems' — but writing detection scripts isn't the same as designing the control framework.

CAATs scripts that flag exceptions are a tool, not a control framework. Sharing them doesn't compromise the auditor's ability to test the underlying transactions, business processes, and other controls.
When IS resources are shared with operations, ask: 'Does the auditor still have independent ways to test what isn't covered by the shared tool?' If yes, sharing is acceptable.
d1_002: A and D feel reasonable (more complex org → more data; familiar org → less data) but neither DRIVES data collection. They are factors that may inform the audit AFTER scope is set.
Purpose, objective, and scope are the audit's north star — every downstream decision (sample size, evidence type, time budget) flows from them.
When you see 'BEST factor for determining the EXTENT' of audit work, look for the option that defines the audit's boundary, not its difficulty or backstory.
d1_003: Trap is A: management is the auditee. Letting them set scope without an independent risk assessment compromises auditor independence — even if their suggestion turns out to be correct.
Management may SUGGEST areas of concern; the auditor must independently VALIDATE through risk assessment. Choice C does both — the assessment may well confirm new systems are highest risk.
Default response when management requests specific scope: thank them, then run a risk assessment. ISACA Standard 1202 makes this mandatory in planning.
d1_004: Audit risk is the umbrella concept: audit risk = inherent × control × detection. The phrase 'during IS auditing' signals the umbrella term, not one of its components.
If the question says 'during the audit / undetected', think audit risk. 'Before any controls' → inherent. 'Controls fail' → control. 'Audit procedures fail' → detection.
ISACA conflates audit risk with material misstatement risk — they're treating the broad 'will I miss something material?' question.
d1_005: Trap is A 'overlapping': sounds related but means TWO controls covering the same objective. That presupposes you have a primary control — in a SoD failure, the primary control is what's missing.
Compensating controls answer: 'We can't implement the ideal control — what else reduces this risk?' Small-team SoD failures almost always demand compensating controls.
Common compensating controls for SoD gaps: enhanced logging + supervisory review, periodic transaction sampling, independent reconciliation, mandatory vacations, job rotation.
d1_006: Trap is C 'fraud detection': it's a real benefit of CSA but a side-effect, not the primary purpose. Don't confuse outcomes with objectives.
CSA's core mechanism is shifting CONTROL OWNERSHIP from audit to business management — making line managers responsible for the controls they live with daily. That's why A wins.
ISACA explicitly distinguishes CSA from internal audit — CSA enhances audit work, it doesn't replace it (immediately rules out D as a 'shift to consultative').
d1_007: Trap is D 'customizable': sounds like the most flexible choice and tools sales pitch favorite. But the PRIMARY requirement is data accuracy without performance impact — customization is nice-to-have.
Auditing tools are 'guests' in production — if the tool degrades the system being audited, the audit itself becomes a business risk and may invalidate the data being captured.
CAATs evaluation order: 1) accuracy of capture → 2) performance impact → 3) compatibility → 4) flexibility/customization.
d1_008: Trap is C 'IT knowledge': feels right (“they know our systems!”). That's exactly the conflict — they have existing relationships and may have worked on the very systems they'd now audit.
Independence is the foundational requirement of any audit role — it overrides all other competencies. Technical knowledge can be acquired; lost independence cannot be restored mid-engagement.
When hiring auditors from operational areas, the screening question is always: 'Which systems and projects did you work on, and which fall under audit scope today?'
d1_009: Trap is A 'CAATs': closely related and effective, but CAATs is a TOOL category. Continuous auditing USES CAATs but adds the real-time + automated reporting layer — the difference matters for 'emerging' risk.
'Emerging' implies time-sensitive: quarterly assessments (B) are too infrequent, log sampling (C) has lag, ad-hoc CAATs (A) still requires you to RUN them on a schedule.
CISA pattern: high transaction volume + emerging risk → continuous auditing. Almost never sampling alone.
d1_010: Two-step distinction: are we testing whether a CONTROL operates correctly (compliance) or whether DATA is accurate (substantive)? 'Were accounts authorized?' is a question about a control — compliance.
Mnemonic: authorization, approval, segregation → compliance. Balances, totals, monetary values → substantive.
A and D are sampling METHODS, not test categories — they self-eliminate when the question asks 'which type of testing is this?'
d1_011: Trap is C 'control': auditors recommend controls but don't implement them. Detection risk is the only risk auditors directly shape — through their choice of procedures, sample size, and expertise.
Risk ownership map: inherent (business nature) → control (management) → detection (auditor) → business (executive/strategy).
Phrase giveaway: 'selection of audit procedures' or 'audit techniques' = detection risk every time.
d1_012: Trap is A 'review prior findings': feels rigorous and IS part of planning, but it's an INPUT to risk assessment, not a substitute. Prior findings tell you about old issues, not current risk landscape.
Risk assessment is the foundation that determines scope, resources, sampling, and procedures. Without it, you're auditing by intuition and exposing the function to coverage gaps.
ISACA Standard 1202 makes risk assessment in planning MANDATORY — not best practice, mandatory. That alone elevates D over the alternatives.
d1_013: Trap is D 'audit core service and dependencies': feels like the right place to dig in, but you can't audit a system you don't yet understand. SOA is a distributed black-box architecture — you must map first, test second.
Canonical sequence for any unfamiliar architecture: documentation review → mapping (services to processes) → controls assessment → transaction testing.
When the question asks for the INITIAL step on a complex system, the answer is almost always 'understand it' — never 'start testing it.'
d1_014: Trap is A 'delete all copies': auditors don't perform remediation. This violates independence (auditor performing operational tasks) and oversteps authority.
Auditor's job: identify → document → report risk to management → recommend prevention. Management decides on remediation, not the auditor.
Anytime an option has the auditor DOING something operational (deleting, blocking, installing, configuring, fixing), it is almost certainly wrong.
d1_015: Trap is B 'state audit objectives': engagement-specific objectives live in the engagement letter, not the charter. The charter is organizational, not project-specific.
The charter is an authority document — it answers 'who, what scope, what authority' for the audit FUNCTION as a whole. Not for individual audits.
Charter content priority: authority > scope > responsibility > reporting line. Procedures (C) and dynamic technology content (A) belong in audit methodology documents, not the charter.
